selected.context: At decision point D2, which position does this researcher hold?
selected.a: Hides the model's reasoning from the training signal to mimic opaque internal reasoning, and tests the distilled (no-CoT) version too, so conclusions apply to models that don't verbalize deception.
selected.b: Uses a control that removes the conflicting objective to check that a behavior (objecting) tracks real misalignment rather than being a generic response to the prompt text.

selected.context: At decision point D2, which position does this researcher hold?
selected.a: Pair every elicitation with a matched baseline (prompt with conflict removed, or fine-tuning on unrelated synthetic documents) so that elevated behavior can be attributed to the manipulated element.
selected.b: prefers making offers to the model real and following through on them over merely fictional promises because credible, honest dealings set a precedent and make the model's responses to the scenario more meaningful.

selected.context: At decision point D2, which position does this researcher hold?
selected.a: Values evidence that is hard for the model to dismiss as a test, e.g., credible offers or deals with hard-to-fake signals placed in the pretraining corpus, with legal or institutional enforcement mechanisms and a track record.
selected.b: Maintains a living, accumulating list of examples, adding new ones as found and later pointing to an updated compilation, treating breadth of independent instances as stronger evidence than any single case.

selected.context: At decision point D3, which position does this researcher hold?
selected.a: Filters generated data to keep only samples that actually exhibit the target behavior before training, so the behavior in the fine-tuning set is verified rather than assumed.
selected.b: Prefers conservative, adversarially-minimised safety estimates (worst case across attack strategies, red team incentivised to win) over average-case results, because the opponent is a potentially scheming model.

selected.context: At decision point D3, which position does this researcher hold?
selected.a: Distrusts evaluations on tasks resembling the model's training distribution, since familiar-format tasks do not reflect the settings where the behavior matters most.
selected.b: Distrusts negative results from tasks where the model can recognize that humans lack demonstrations, since a failure to show deception in itself would not imply absence of deception.

proposals.principle: Prefers hiding the model's reasoning from the training signal and testing the distilled no-CoT version over a control-based check, because conclusions should generalize to models that do not verbalize deception.

Prefers designs that test whether the behavior holds in models that never verbalize their reasoning over designs that only verify the behavior tracks misalignment rather than generic prompt responses.

Prefers pairing each elicitation with a matched baseline (conflict removed or unrelated synthetic fine-tuning) over making offers real, because attributing elevated behavior to the manipulated element requires a controlled comparison.
Prefers controlled baselines that isolate the manipulated element over realistic, honest dealings with the model, because causal attribution is the main goal of the experiment.
Prefers a living, accumulating list of independent examples over a single high-credibility deal, because breadth of independent instances is stronger evidence than any one case.
Prefers breadth of independent examples that can be updated over single cases hard to dismiss as tests, because cumulative evidence is more robust than one artifact.

Prefers filtering generated fine-tuning data to keep only samples verified to exhibit the target behavior over assuming it is present, because verified training data makes the trained behavior reliable.
Prefers verifying target behavior in the fine-tuning data over conservative worst-case safety estimates, because grounding training in confirmed examples is more immediately actionable.
Prefers distrusting negative results on tasks where humans lack demonstrations over distrusting familiar-format evaluations, because a failure to show deception does not establish its absence.

Prefers treating null results as uninformative when the model could recognize the absence of human demonstrations over treating distribution similarity as the main validity concern, because the recognition gap undermines the test itself.
